# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.

Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". lines: **What it is** — Under "The Delayed Training Effect and Long Duration Work," the authors state: "With respect to aerobic and anaerobic productivity, there is no experimental data that clearly documents occurrence of the LDTE phenomenon in cyclic distance training. The exceptions are cases of intense training under the lowered oxygen conditions of high altitude" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image). Their evidence:

- **Swimmers (Vaitsekhovsky et al 1974).** "significant increases" in "maximum aerobic capacity, the total volume of work which can be executed at the critical level of power, VO2 max and the onset of blood lactate accumulation." "These changes persisted for more than 4 weeks after 3 weeks of training at an altitude of 1700m above sea level, with a peak response taking place about 1 week after the altitude training. All of the athletes in the study improved their results immediately after training at altitude."

- **Skaters (Ivanov 1977).** A 4-minute cycle-ergometer test weekly for 3 weeks at 2250 m, then for 3 weeks at sea level. At altitude, mechanical efficiency fell and oxygen consumption, energy expenditure and lactate rose; back at sea level, "the functional efficiency of the work exceeded the pre-experimental levels as a result of more economical metabolism and a significantly diminished amount of anaerobically produced ATP" (same page).

-- **Not an altitude case: swimmers under large loads at sea level (Susman 1978).** The authors cite this as evidence that load-induced homeostatic disturbance shows in psycho-physiological indicators, not as a documented LDTE. Large loads slowed "complex motor reactions," reduced precision of movement patterns and of "tracking a moving object," and lowered work capacity, ECG-assessed cardiovascular state, muscle tonus and adrenal-cortex hormone levels. After loads were reduced and intensity altered, these indicators rose "as the supercompensation (adaptive reconstruction) phase emerged" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image).

+- **Not an altitude case: swimmers under large loads (Susman 1978; no altitude is mentioned).** The authors cite this as evidence that load-induced homeostatic disturbance shows in psycho-physiological indicators, not as a documented LDTE. Large loads slowed "complex motor reactions," reduced precision of movement patterns and of "tracking a moving object," and lowered work capacity, ECG-assessed cardiovascular state, muscle tonus and adrenal-cortex hormone levels. After loads were reduced and intensity altered, these indicators rose "as the supercompensation (adaptive reconstruction) phase emerged" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for the altitude cases: hypobaric conditions gave "a very demanding training influence which provoked persistent disturbance of the body's homeostasis and subsequent activation of its adaptive processes" (PDF p. 376). For why the LDTE is not seen at sea level, they hedge: if it exists there, the disturbance "will occur at the level of more subtle physiological systems" not detectable by "methods used for assessing the more gross aerobic and anaerobic processes," and "adaptation apparently occurs at deeper cellular and molecular levels (e.g. in the mitochondria and endocrine system)" (Yakovlev 1957, 1974; Viru 1969, 1981; Finogenov 1979), while "disturbance of homeostasis can be detected in the dynamics of a number of psycho-physiological indicators" of the central nervous and neuromuscular systems (PDF pp. 376-377). This is a stated hypothesis, not a demonstrated mechanism.

4	SUPERTRAINING
5	One can even establish an aerobics class circuit without the need for fixed stations spread around a 
6	gymnasium. The instructor can then structure the class so that each person does a sequence of free-standing 
7	exercises or movements using strap-on ankle/wrist weights according to the structure of a circuit such as any one 
8	of those depicted in Figures 5.21 to 5.24. Instead of following the traditional approach of doing every exercise to 
9	completion for several dozen repetitions, one executes a set sequence of, say, ten exercises for a fixed number of 
10	excursions through the circuit. The aerobics class may easily consist of two or three discrete circuits to be 
11	performed in the same session, depending on the level of fitness of the participants. In such a case, circuit 1 may 
12	be a flexibility circuit; circuit 2 may be a muscle endurance circuit; and the final circuit may be an aerobic circuit.
13	Concluding C om m ents
14	The above information was presented to evaluate the merits and limitations of traditional circuits in order that a 
15	far more extensive and useful concept of continuous and interval circuit training could be developed. It by no 
16	means exhausts the full repertoire of available theory and practical applications, but it furnishes necessary and 
17	sufficient material to enable the instructor to create effective, appropriate, safe and entertaining circuit training 
18	programmes.
19	A final word of advice is probably necessary for the instructor. The design o f any circuit training programme 
20	is incomplete if attention is paid to the single session alone. A long-term plan has to be drawn up in which the 
21	type, duration, intensity and complexity of each circuit is changed to facilitate the development of the necessary' 
22	fitness factors. In particular, the principles of supcrcompensation and pcriodisation have to be applied to ensure 
23	that progress is optimised and injury is minimised. For example, it would be advisable to ensure that light and 
24	heavy circuits alternate, with provision being made for adequate restoration by means of active and passive rest 
25	periods or days.
26	If this type of scientific planning is observed, the instructor should be able to ensure that this extended circuit 
27	training system will be of definite benefit to all participants during all stages of their fitness programmes. It 
28	should always be remembered that all forms o f circuit training are largely suited to the average non-athlete or 
29	competitive athlete during the early preparatory phase o f training. The constant progression in a circuit from one 
30	exercise to another without completing all sets with one exercise to a prescribed maximum number of repetitions 
31	before moving to the next exercise does not permit one to adequately develop the different types of sport specific 
32	strength. Even with interval circuit training on machines, it is not possible to train with the medium heavy, near 
33	maximal or explosive loading which is necessary to develop qualities such as muscle hypertrophy, speed-strength, 
34	strcngth-speed, static strength, flexibility-strength, explosive strength and acceleration strength. The length of the 
35	interval between successive sets of the same exercise depends on the number of stations in the circuit, so the larger 
36	the circuit, the less its ability to significantly develop any of the major sport-specific strength-related qualities.

41	SUPERTRAINING
42	PROGRAMMING AND 
43	ORGANISATION OF TRAINING
44	6.1 The Development of Training Organisation
45	The organisation of the training process is fundamental to all highly competitive sports today, being responsible 
46	for the exceptional performances produced by modem athletes. 
47	The need for proper organisation for physical 
48	fitness is not new; it was an essential part of preparation for warfare in many ancient cultures such as China, 
49	Greece and Rome, since their ability to survive depended largely on the military capabilities of their armies (see 
50	Ch 1). In the formalised sports setting, the Greeks of more than two thousand years ago prepared for the Olympic 
51	Games by allocating a preparatory training period of at least 10 months a year.
52	The organisation of training into phases of different types of exercise done at varying intensity and volume, 
53	however, is a much more recent development which gained a great deal of impetus near the beginning of the 
54	20th century when researchers began to probe human physiology and psychology with an enthusiasm which has 
55	not yet abated. Scientists such as Pavlov studied how the body adapts to environmental stimuli and the idea of 
56	conditioning soon became an integral part of understanding adaptation.
57	The foundations of modem training organisation and periodisation were laid in the Soviet Union at about the 
58	time of the Russian revolution. One of the earliest texts on this subject was written by Kotov (Olympic Sport, 
59	1917), who considered it appropriate to divide training into general, preparatory and specific stages. The general 
60	stage was aimed at developing the vegetative (cardiovascular-respiratory) and muscular systems, while 
61	preparatory training of about two months' duration was devoted to improving strength and muscle endurance. 
62	The specific stage was used to prepare the athlete for a given sporting event in two parts: initial and main 
63	training, both of about four months' duration, but there was still no overall methodology of periodisation in the 
64	form of definite cycles of different types of training.
65	The preliminary steps towards establishing this methodology appeared a few years later in two books: 
66	Scientific Foundations o f Training by Gorinewsky (1922) and The Basis o f Training by Birsin (1925). Some of 
67	the first practical applications of early periodisation were made in track-and-field by Vsorov (Basic Principles o f 
68	Training Athletes, Moscow, 1938), in skiing by Bergman ( Training programmes and Periods o f Training in 
69	Siding, Moscow, 1938), in gymnastics by Korijakovsky (Gymnastics, Moscow, 1938), in boxing by Gradopolov 
70	[Manual o f Boxing, Moscow, 1938) and in water sports by Shuvalov (Swimming. Waterpolo, Diving, Moscow, 
71	1940).
72	In Finland, Pikhala had already published his treatise called Athletism (1930), which drew up a series of 
73	basic principles, especially the prevention of overtraining by using an undulating rhythm of training which 
74	alternates periods of work and rest. Like many other authors at the time, his planning was founded upon the 
75	traditional importance of climatic seasons, rather than quantitatively determined phases of loading.
76	At about the same time, research findings and the practical experience of athletes were assembled by Grantyn 
77	in an article 'Contents and General Foundations of Training Preparation' 
78	(Teoriya i Praktika Fizischeskoi 
79	Kultury, Moscow, 1939: 7). In it, he divided the annual training cycle into three periods: preparatory, main and 
80	transitional, with the transitional period comprising two stages, namely a gradual detraining to rest, followed by 
81	active rest using methods of general physical preparation at reduced intensity. Other sports such as gymnastics 
82	and jogging were recommended as suitable for the transition period, thereby already suggesting the role of 
83	combinational training' as a form of restoration and predating the commercialised idea of'cross training' by many 
84	decades.
85	The importance of considering the competitive calendar and climatic factors in periodising training was 
86	stressed by Ozolin in his important text Training the Athlete (Moscow, 1949). In it he also emphasized that 
87	active rest should form an integral part of the transition phase to maintain and improve preparedness. This view 
88	m supported by the research of Hettinger and Muller in 1955, who found that lowest trainability occurred 
89	dunng the winter months and highest trainability took place in summer and autumn, with a sharp drop in 
90	trainability at the onset of winter (Hettinger, 1961). This work suggested that the changes seemed to coincide 
91	with changes in the levels of ultraviolet radiation, especially since exposure of athletes to artificial ultraviolet
92	6
93	313
94	
95	
96	######## PDF idx 325 (printed 314) ########
97	SUPERTRAINING
98	light during the winter eliminated the observed changcs in trainability. In fact, the book by Hettinger which 
99	quoted these studies (7he Physiology o f Strength), like some of the early work by DeLorme, still remains one of 
100	the best pioneering texts on popularised scientific strength training, with the team of Hettinger and Muller 
101	undertaking many studies which were often well ahead of their time.
102	Another useful contribution was made by Letunov, who wrote an article ’Reflections on the Systematk 
103	Formulation of Training’ (Sovietsky Sport, 1950: 125) which strongly criticised the formulation of training 
104	regimes on the basis of the competition calendar alone. He felt that the stages of training were a consequence of 
105	biological processes, although he failed to appreciate that these processes, in turn, were modified by the training 
106	loads.
107	In England, Dyson was one of the first Westerners to popularise periodisation by using his knowledge of 
108	Eastern and Western training methods to write a textbook A New System o f Training (1946), which delineated a 
109	five-phase system of pcriodisation for athletics:
110	1. Non-competitive preparation period (5 months) with activities like gym training and cross-country running
111	2. Pre-competitive period, the beginning of specific preparation (1 month).
112	3. Initial competitive period (6 weeks).
113	4. Main competitive period (6 weeks).
114	5. Post-competitive period (6 weeks).
115	Ways of Organising Training
116	The above summary of the emergence of periodisation as a means of organising training may create the 
117	impression that periodisation is the only type of organisation or that it is synonymous with the organisation or 
118	scheduling of training. This is far from the truth, since there are numerous ways of preparing an athlete for 
119	competition and classical methods of periodisation may not necessarily offer the best approach to training 
120	organisation. Training for all sport may be carried out in terms of two broad general categories:
121	• Use of the sport alone to develop fitness for the given sport
122	• Use of the sport and supplementary activities to develop fitness for the given sport.
123	In the first case, training uses both the sport as a entire entity and the various aspects of the sport to enhance 
124	fitness, such as selected movements and portions of the play. In the latter case, supplementary activities such as 
125	resistance training, running and jumping may be used to develop the most important fitness qualities (e.g. speed, 
126	speed-strength or muscular endurance) demanded by the sport. Today, the idea of 'cross training' with other 
127	sports is also popular for achieving this aim. Most of the supplementary training is usually carried out before the 
128	competitive season begins, with intermittent use of such training in small doses to maintain the specific fitness 
129	qualities. Both of these categories of training require some or other form of organisation, one of the approaches 
130	being to rely strictly on periodisation.
131	Whichever system of organisation is chosen, the underlying principle to be applied is that o f optimal stress 
132	and restoration (see 1.16). This entails designing a physical training programme which stresses the body in such 
133	a way as to cause the appropriate form of supercompensatory adaptation, facilitated by regular use of restorative 
134	means to optimise the process and by regular enhancement of motor skills through nervous stimulation. To 
135	summarise what was covered in detail in 1.16, each training stimulus acts as a stressor which causes an acute 
136	(short-term) and a delayed response. If the stressor is of suitable intensity and duration, the restorative measures 
137	are adequate and subsequent stimuli (in the workout, microcycle or mesocycle) are applied at the most 
138	advantageous time of the stress recovery curve, then supercompensation and adaptation at a higher level of 
139	performance will follow. With special regard to strength training, Hettinger (1961) pointed out the following 
140	features of training which stimulate supcrcompcnsation. It is interesting to note that, although these points have 
141	been modified and extended by more recent research, they still offer useful information for the general strength 
142	training world today:
143	1. Production of adequate muscle tension is central to all muscic training
144	2. The maximum training benefits are derived by using muscle tension of no less than 40-50% of one’s 1RM
145	3. Maximum training effect does not require prolonging muscle tension to the point of fatigue
146	4. One single maximal strength effort per day is sufficient to maintain progress
147	Division of the sporting year into preparatory and competitive phases emerged logically from the experience of 
148	coaches and athletes, a distinction which creates the false impression that no preparation occurs during the
149	314
150	
151	
152	######## PDF idx 326 (printed 315) ########
153	SUPERTRAINING
154	competitive phase and no competition occurs during the preparatory phase. In team sports or track-and-field, the 
155	season is often so prolonged that this distinction cannot always be applied with such purity. Competitions may 
156	serve as a form of testing, controlled training or specific preparation; moreover, there are regular transition phases 
157	between preparatory stages and competitions over a prolonged season.
158	It can also be misleading to state categorically that there is a generalised training model for each sport. As 
159	in all scientific disciplines, several models may be possible, depending on many factors, including the situation, 
160	the individual, the variables and the period. Effective modem programming is a science and art which involves 
161	creativity, flexibility, individuality and understanding. Contingency plans should also be available to cope with 
162	unexpected or unplanned situations such as injury, loss of motivation, premature stagnation, changes in the rules, 
163	changes in the competitive roster, and personal trauma.
164	Implementation of the principle of specificity (see 1.3) is vital to the success of training, with high intensity 
165	sport-specific training under competitive circumstances (known as event-specific training) during both the 
166	preparatory and competition phases being an integral part of the programme. 
167	It is inadequate to train 
168	conservatively throughout the preparatory stage and the early competitive phase, deliberately avoiding stressful 
169	competitive situations in an attempt to produce maximal supercompensation with minimum injury by a specific 
170	date. Part of sport specific preparation is training under conditions which simulate those of the actual event so 
171	that one can cope efficiently with the demands of competition.
172	The precise balance between event-specific, sport-specific and general training is determined by the type of 
173	sport and the individual. For example, supplementary training (sport-specific and general training) for speed- 
174	strength and strength sports should constitute about 50-60% of the total work, whereas in distance endurance 
175	events, this type of training should constitute no more than about 20-30% of the work load.
176	Considerable research and experience has shown that the system of using the sport alone to develop 
177	proficiency generally is less effective than the integrated system of sport and supplementary training, although 
178	there seem to be notable exceptions in certain sports such as gymnastics. However, this is not necessarily an 
179	indictment of the use of strength training in some situations; more often than not it reflects a lack of adequate 
180	information and experience in this regard. The main ways in which an adjunct strength training system may be 
181	applied are as follows:
182	• Non-quantitative supplementary training consisting of general preparatory exercises precedes the competitive 
183	period, during which predominantly event-specific training is done. No calculations of training intensity or 
184	volume are made for prescribing the stages of training, although sports results or IRMs may be used to 
185	modify the programme.
186	• Non-quantitativc supplementary training comprising a general preparatory phase and a special preparatory 
187	phase precedes the competitive phase, during which predominantly event-specific training is done. No 
188	calculations of training intensity or volume are made for prescribing and monitoring the various stages of 
189	training, although sports results or IRMs may be used to modify the programme.
190	• Some form of long-term pcriodisation is applied. Calculations of training intensity and volume arc made to 
191	ensure that certain performance goals are attained at given stages of the long-term programme.
192	Before any serious discussion on periodisation begins, it is relevant to deal with the contention by 
193	some 
194	authorities that this cycled method of training organisation is unnecessary. It is quite true that many athletes have 
195	excelled with other methods, but this is not to say that all variants of periodisation need to be dismissed out of 
196	hand. On the contrary, some Western research which regards periodisation as a special version of the progressive 
197	overload principle is now beginning to corroborate the findings of Russian workers. The alternation o f heavy, 
198	medium and light days and phases alone would appear to facilitate recovery and adaptation to heavy loading 
199	more effectively than the use of monotonic increasing loading from phase to phase. Here, the heavy training days 
200	would strongly activate the relevant muscles, while the alternate lower intensity days would minimise the chance 
201	of overtraining or impaired restoration (Fry et al, 1994a; Fry et al, 1994b). Other research has shown the 
202	importance of periodising variations in training, especially as the latter becomes more demanding (Kraemer & 
203	Koziris 1992, Kraemer & Koziris 1994, Hakinnen 1989, Hakinnen & Komi 1986, Hakinnen & Pakarincn 1993a, 
204	Hakinnen & Pakarinen 1993b).
205	315
206	
207	
208	######## PDF idx 327 (printed 316) ########
209	SUPERTRAINING
210	6.2 Periodisation as a Form of Organisation
211	As defined briefly in earlier chapters, the overall long-term cyclic structuring of training and practice to maximise 
212	performance to coincide with important competitions is known as periodisation (sec 1.14, 5.3 and 5.4).
213	Definitions and Fundamental Concepts
214	It is interesting to note that at least one Biblical quotation contains in colloquial terms some of the mos 
215	fundamental concepts of periodisation or cycled training, namely Ecclesiastes 3:
216	"There is a time for everything and a season fo r every activity under heaven . . .
217	A time to tear down and a time to build. . .
218	A time to search atui a time to give up . . .
219	A time to keep and a time to throw away.
220	A time to tear and a time to mend . .. "
221	The periodisation approach organises all training in terms of several basic structural units, namely the training 
222	session (the fundamental unit), the training day, the microcycle, the mesocycle, the macrocycle, the Olympic (or 
223	quadrennial) cycle and the multi-year cycle.
224	The microcycle refers to a number of training sessions which form a recurrent unit with a period of several 
225	days. 
226	Its minimum content is two different types of workout. 
227	The training day comprises one or more 
228	interrelated training sessions, with Bulgarian weightliftcrs commonly using in excess of 5 sessions per day, six 
229	days a week, each session comprising a few key exercises. The ntesocycle refers to a number of microcycles 
230	which serve as a recurring unit over a period of several weeks or months, while a macrocycle (which refers to a 
231	single competitive season) comprises a number of mcsocycles occupying a period of many months. It should be 
232	noted that earlier Russian literature, in contravention of the meaning of the prefixes meso- (middle) and macro- 
233	(large), used the term macrocycle to refer to what is now known as a mesocycle and vice versa. Any reader who 
234	may concurrently be referring to older Russian material should bear in mind that the above linguistically 
235	corrected meanings for the various training cycles are used in this text. The multi-year plan usually refers to a 
236	period exceeding that of the Olympic cycle.
237	More quantitatively, the microcycle typically has a duration of about 5-10 days; the mesocycle, a duration of 
238	1-4 months; and the macrocycle, 10-12 months. The term 'large macrocycle' sometimes is also used and may 
239	refer, for instance, to the training period of four years between successive Olympic Games or the several years 
240	taken to raise the level of qualification of an athlete from one Class to the next highest. Multi-year planning can 
241	include the latter type of macrocycle, but more characteristically, this term refers to the long-term organisation of 
242	an athlete's career as a junior or senior competitor or of the athlete's entire competitive lifespan. Three major 
243	phases of all training are recognised conventionally: preparation, competition and post-competition.
244	The contents and characteristics of each cycle are determined by the specific goals or results desired at the 
245	end of the cycle concerned. One has to be extremely carefully not to devise training units or programmes which 
246	try to develop any motor abilities or types of fitness which interfere with one another, as has been discussed 
247	earlier. Sometimes the coach may also attempt to develop too many or all types of fitness required by a given 
248	sport, thereby contravening the heterochronicity principle of development of the different motor abilities (see 
249	2.2.3 and later 6.10).
250	Various transition phases are often recognised between each of the major phases, with the post-competition 
251	phase often being regarded as the main transition phase, being used mainly for restoration. Some authorities 
252	consider that one of the transition phases should be recognised as a conversion phase during which specialised 
253	training converts maximum strength either into speed-strcngth or strength-cndurance. Although this terminology 
254	superficially seems attractive and descriptive, it is scientifically inaccurate, since one type of strength or motor 
255	ability cannot change into another, as has been shown by considerable research into the specificity of adaptation. 
256	It is more accurate to state that a prior stage of maximal strength training may serve as the foundation upon which 
257	later training for speed-strength or endurance is based, a sequence which is fundamental to some systems of 
258	training, e.g. the conjugate sequence system (see 5.3).

260	uniformly increasing loading), introductory (bringing the athlete up to the competition stage), restorative (after 
261	heavy loading), competitive (immediately before and including the competition), and shock or stress (stimulating 
262	the athlete out of a state of stagnation) microcycles (Matveyev, 1981). Shock microcycles typically arc used if

283	athlete recover after heavy loading. Sometimes, the restorative-maintenance mesocyclc is simply referred to as a

285	experts recognise large mesocycles, which comprise a closely integrated system of smaller mesocycles each of 
286	which has specific training goals. Later in this text, the concept of concentrated loading mesocycles is covered in

289	preparatory phase for long-duration endurance sports may use the following scheme:

295	Preparatory Phases of Training
296	As implied by the above discussion on mesocycles, the preparatory phase may be broken down further into GPP 
297	(General Physical Preparation) and SPP (Specialised Physical Preparation). 
298	However, it should always be 
299	remembered that the GPP and SPP always form an interconnected unit. In some cases, the GPP and SPP may 
300	even be concurrent or the GPP may be largely indistinguishable from the SPP (Bondarchuk, 1979).
301	The GPP is intended to provide balanced physical conditioning in endurance, strength, speed, flexibility and 
302	other basic factors of fitness, whereas the SPP concentrates on exercises which are more specific to the particular 
303	sport. 
304	Characteristically, the GPP may include participation in a variety of different physical activities which 
305	provide low intensity, all-round conditioning, with little emphasis on specific sporting skills. Participation in 
306	activities such as jogging, swimming, cycling, tennis or volleyball may be appropriate in this phase for some 
307	sports. If the player needs to gain muscle or lose excess fat, this is regarded as the appropriate period to do so. 
308	Sometimes an hypertrophy phase may be included in the GPP if there is a need for gaining functional muscle 
309	bulk. The decision to utilise this type of phase should be based on an assessment of the strength deficit discussed 
310	previously (Ch 1 and Fig 1.1).
311	Sometimes it is important to include very specific SPP-type exercises during the GPP either to rehabilitate 
312	any existing injuries or to eliminate any structural or functional deficiencies or imbalances in physique, posture 
313	and ncuromuscular skill. It may also be relevant to curtail or eliminate standard types of GPP from the training 
314	programme of anyone who is an advanced athlete or has trained regularly for a prolonged period at increasing 
315	levels of proficiency. Similarly, the use of GPP-type exercises may be appropriate for brief periods during the 
316	SPF to facilitate recovery or prevent stagnation. Moreover, the methods of GPP training are unsuitable for 
317	adequately or timeously stimulating improvements in performance among advanced athletes, whose trainability 
318	has already waned considerably over years of competition and whose continued growth depends on more specific 
319	or demanding methods.

325	Some transition phases, especially those following the end of a training season, may display many of the 
326	characteristics of a typical GPP. However, one should be careful not to allow prolonged GPP type training during 
327	any transition phases to diminish the sport specific fitness of the athlete.
328	According to the more traditional schemes of periodisation, the volume o f loading should be high during 
329	GPP and its intensity low, then a gradual transition to SPP should occur, during which the exercise volume should 
330	decrease and its intensity should increase (Fig 6.1). At the same time, increasing emphasis should be laid on 
331	developing the sport specific fitness factors such as speed-strength, flexibility-strcngth, static endurance and 
332	dynamic flexibility, as well as the specific skills required by the particular player. Appropriate variations should 
333	be introduced during this phase to ensure progress and motivation.
334	Further Phases and Principles
335	Near the beginning of the competitive season, a stabilisation phase may be commenced to ensure that the various 
336	fitness qualities developed in the off-season arc maintained throughout the season. It is important to remember 
337	that the average athlete usually has little desire to spend hours in a gymnasium or undertaking 'cross training’. 
338	Consequently, it is often recommended that stabilisation training generally needs to occupy a short period before 
339	or during practice or preferably twice a week for no more than 30 minutes in a gymnasium, using a limited 
340	number of major multi-joint exercises. 
341	Some of the basic strengthening and flexibility exercises may be 
342	integrated into normal practice sessions, using partners to offer resistance, if necessary.
343	The gradual overload principle, with periodic underloading days or microcycles, is constantly adhered to 
344	through all training cycles to ensure that an adequate, but not excessive, training stimulus is imposed on the body. 
345	A preliminary recommendation is that individual workouts should generally be alternated in terms of light, 
346	medium and heavy loading to guard against overtraining and to ensure optimal training and competitive 
347	efficiency. This variation in training load on a daily, microcyclic and mesocyclic basis is essential for avoiding 
348	stagnation. In this respect, it is common to observe the well-known empirical Rule o f Sixty Percent, which states 
349	that the training volume of any stage (day or microcycle) with light loading should be approximately 60% of the 
350	volume of a stage with heavy (maximal or near-maximal) loading.
351	Acquisition and Stabilisation of Technical Skills
352	Even the most meticulous computation and prescription of load intensity, volume and sequencing that optimally 
353	develops work capacity is of little conscqucnce to performance if changes in technical mastery are not constantly 
354	monitored. Laboratory tests may reveal excellent maximal strength, VO2 max, muscle endurance, reaction times 
355	and so forth, but they simply identify the potential offered by the athlete's work capacity and not functional 
356	preparedness, which relies on the mastery of specific motor skills to produce top-level performance.
357	Thus, it is essential to quantitatively monitor progressive changes in technical skill. One way of doing this is 
358	to record the athlete’s reliability o f technique by keeping a record of the percentages of successes experienced in 
359	executing the same specific skills during training and competition. Reliability often changes under different 
360	conditions, so that it is valuable to keep a record of competitive reliability versus training reliability. A low 
361	competitive reliability relative to training reliability indicates that the athlete probably has difficulty in 
362	performing under conditions of high emotional excitement and needs to simulate those conditions during training. 
363	The term 'gym lifters' has been applied for many years to lifters who can lift much more in training than on the 
364	platform. In this case it is apparent that emotional stress during competition exerts a negative effect, not on the 
365	obviously adequate levels of strength or power, but on the technical skills required.
366	Progression to more difficult skills should not occur until the reliability at the preceding level of complexity 
367	or intensity has stabilised at a level of at least 70-80%, where zones of intensity or complexity are formally laid 
368	down for each aspect of a given sport. This method is sometimes called the zone-by-zone mastering o f intensity 
369	(Matveyev, 1977). It stresses the importance of:
370	• eliminating any factors from training which disrupt learning of technique
371	• the premature introduction of skills for an athlete of a certain qualification
372	• the ability to master mental control and attitudes towards complex, demanding or fearful tasks
373	Consequently, it is vital to monitor reliability of technique at all stages of short- and long-term planning and 
374	organisation. Sometimes, loss of form is prematurely attributed to overtraining or deficient training, but in many 
375	cases, the problem may lie in inadequate attention being paid to the regular monitoring and cyclical variation of

461	Matveyev, in addressing other issues concerning so-called transition mesocycles, posed the intriguing 
462	question: “Why not retain sporting form permanently as a state which is optimal for the athlete?” This would

465	model, thereby suggesting that one must be very circumspect before taking any training model at face value.
466	He answers his own question by stating that retention of the same sporting form ignores the fact that the same 
467	training stressors which contribute positively to an athlete’s fitness over a certain period can become negative 
468	stressors if used for too long, since adaptation is a characteristic of all life and variety ensures growth. Moreover, 
469	the sporting form needed for reaching another level of performance requires further different adaptive 
470	reconstruction of all systems of the body, since sporting form which may be optimal for a given stage of 
471	performance is not optimal for the next stage of performance. Thus, he is clearly pointing out the need for regular 
472	updating of any periodisation or organisational training model or even changing to another one which may differ 
473	radically from that of a previous stage in an athlete’s career.

531	6.2.2 Calculation of the Parameters of Periodisation
532	The effective prescription and organisation of training depends on calculating the most important parameters of 
533	loading. Conventionally, the most frequently computed parameters are the volume and intensity of the load, 
534	where volume is intended to provide some measure of the total work done over a given period and intensity is a 
535	measure of the average force exerted. The precise methods of physics are not applied, because of their greater 
536	complexity for the average coach or competitor; instead, approximate measures which correlate closely with the 
537	physically computed values are used.
538	Thus, volume of any exercise is calculated (in kilograms) by multiplying the weight lifted by the number of 
539	repetitions at that weight. The total volume for a workout is the sum of the volumes calculated for all the major 
540	exercises. Some authorities (Chernyak, 1978) stipulate that only weights of greater than 40% of IRM should be 
541	taken into account when performing these calculations, since the strengthening effects of lighter weights than this 
542	is minimal.
543	Often, the quantity of lifts is calculated by adding together the total number of lifts done. The intensity of a 
544	given exercise is calculated by dividing the volume of that exercise by the number of repetitions executed for that 
545	exercise. The intensity of a workout is the total volume of all the major exercises divided by the total number of 
546	lifts in the workout, i.e. it is the average weight lifted in a given workout or period. Generally, except for 
547	beginners, warmup sets with loads of less than about 70% of 1 RM are not included in the calculations. The 
548	following example shows how these parameters are calculated for Exercise A done for four sets (the first figure is 
549	the load; the second figure, the number of repetitions):

553	The first set with 60kg (i.e. 50% of IRM) is ignored, since it constitutes a warmup. Thus:
554	Volume Va = 640 + 400 + 220 
555	= 1260kg 
556	Total reps Ra = 14

563	use of overall averages can be very misleading in prescribing training, since they give no indication of the range 
564	of loads used. For instance, the relative intensity of the four sets of Exercise A (75%) is below what may be 
565	classed as a heavy workout, even though the heaviest load used was 110kg (92% of IRM). The same relative 
566	intensity could be achieved by executing 3 identical sets each with 75kg for 3 repetitions. Obviously this would 
567	be far less demanding than the former regime. Thus, the overall demands of training must always be examined

SUPERTRAINING
One can even establish an aerobics class circuit without the need for fixed stations spread around a 
gymnasium. The instructor can then structure the class so that each person does a sequence of free-standing 
exercises or movements using strap-on ankle/wrist weights according to the structure of a circuit such as any one 
of those depicted in Figures 5.21 to 5.24. Instead of following the traditional approach of doing every exercise to 
completion for several dozen repetitions, one executes a set sequence of, say, ten exercises for a fixed number of 
excursions through the circuit. The aerobics class may easily consist of two or three discrete circuits to be 
performed in the same session, depending on the level of fitness of the participants. In such a case, circuit 1 may 
be a flexibility circuit; circuit 2 may be a muscle endurance circuit; and the final circuit may be an aerobic circuit.
Concluding C om m ents
The above information was presented to evaluate the merits and limitations of traditional circuits in order that a 
far more extensive and useful concept of continuous and interval circuit training could be developed. It by no 
means exhausts the full repertoire of available theory and practical applications, but it furnishes necessary and 
sufficient material to enable the instructor to create effective, appropriate, safe and entertaining circuit training 
programmes.
A final word of advice is probably necessary for the instructor. The design o f any circuit training programme 
is incomplete if attention is paid to the single session alone. A long-term plan has to be drawn up in which the 
type, duration, intensity and complexity of each circuit is changed to facilitate the development of the necessary' 
fitness factors. In particular, the principles of supcrcompensation and pcriodisation have to be applied to ensure 
that progress is optimised and injury is minimised. For example, it would be advisable to ensure that light and 
heavy circuits alternate, with provision being made for adequate restoration by means of active and passive rest 
periods or days.
If this type of scientific planning is observed, the instructor should be able to ensure that this extended circuit 
training system will be of definite benefit to all participants during all stages of their fitness programmes. It 
should always be remembered that all forms o f circuit training are largely suited to the average non-athlete or 
competitive athlete during the early preparatory phase o f training. The constant progression in a circuit from one 
exercise to another without completing all sets with one exercise to a prescribed maximum number of repetitions 
before moving to the next exercise does not permit one to adequately develop the different types of sport specific 
strength. Even with interval circuit training on machines, it is not possible to train with the medium heavy, near 
maximal or explosive loading which is necessary to develop qualities such as muscle hypertrophy, speed-strength, 
strcngth-speed, static strength, flexibility-strength, explosive strength and acceleration strength. The length of the 
interval between successive sets of the same exercise depends on the number of stations in the circuit, so the larger 
the circuit, the less its ability to significantly develop any of the major sport-specific strength-related qualities.

PROGRAMMING AND 
ORGANISATION OF TRAINING
6.1 The Development of Training Organisation
The organisation of the training process is fundamental to all highly competitive sports today, being responsible 
for the exceptional performances produced by modem athletes. 
The need for proper organisation for physical 
fitness is not new; it was an essential part of preparation for warfare in many ancient cultures such as China, 
Greece and Rome, since their ability to survive depended largely on the military capabilities of their armies (see 
Ch 1). In the formalised sports setting, the Greeks of more than two thousand years ago prepared for the Olympic 
Games by allocating a preparatory training period of at least 10 months a year.
The organisation of training into phases of different types of exercise done at varying intensity and volume, 
however, is a much more recent development which gained a great deal of impetus near the beginning of the 
20th century when researchers began to probe human physiology and psychology with an enthusiasm which has 
not yet abated. Scientists such as Pavlov studied how the body adapts to environmental stimuli and the idea of 
conditioning soon became an integral part of understanding adaptation.
The foundations of modem training organisation and periodisation were laid in the Soviet Union at about the 
time of the Russian revolution. One of the earliest texts on this subject was written by Kotov (Olympic Sport, 
1917), who considered it appropriate to divide training into general, preparatory and specific stages. The general 
stage was aimed at developing the vegetative (cardiovascular-respiratory) and muscular systems, while 
preparatory training of about two months' duration was devoted to improving strength and muscle endurance. 
The specific stage was used to prepare the athlete for a given sporting event in two parts: initial and main 
training, both of about four months' duration, but there was still no overall methodology of periodisation in the 
form of definite cycles of different types of training.
The preliminary steps towards establishing this methodology appeared a few years later in two books: 
Scientific Foundations o f Training by Gorinewsky (1922) and The Basis o f Training by Birsin (1925). Some of 
the first practical applications of early periodisation were made in track-and-field by Vsorov (Basic Principles o f 
Training Athletes, Moscow, 1938), in skiing by Bergman ( Training programmes and Periods o f Training in 
Siding, Moscow, 1938), in gymnastics by Korijakovsky (Gymnastics, Moscow, 1938), in boxing by Gradopolov 
[Manual o f Boxing, Moscow, 1938) and in water sports by Shuvalov (Swimming. Waterpolo, Diving, Moscow, 
1940).
In Finland, Pikhala had already published his treatise called Athletism (1930), which drew up a series of 
basic principles, especially the prevention of overtraining by using an undulating rhythm of training which 
alternates periods of work and rest. Like many other authors at the time, his planning was founded upon the 
traditional importance of climatic seasons, rather than quantitatively determined phases of loading.
At about the same time, research findings and the practical experience of athletes were assembled by Grantyn 
in an article 'Contents and General Foundations of Training Preparation' 
(Teoriya i Praktika Fizischeskoi 
Kultury, Moscow, 1939: 7). In it, he divided the annual training cycle into three periods: preparatory, main and 
transitional, with the transitional period comprising two stages, namely a gradual detraining to rest, followed by 
active rest using methods of general physical preparation at reduced intensity. Other sports such as gymnastics 
and jogging were recommended as suitable for the transition period, thereby already suggesting the role of 
combinational training' as a form of restoration and predating the commercialised idea of'cross training' by many 
decades.
The importance of considering the competitive calendar and climatic factors in periodising training was 
stressed by Ozolin in his important text Training the Athlete (Moscow, 1949). In it he also emphasized that 
active rest should form an integral part of the transition phase to maintain and improve preparedness. This view 
m supported by the research of Hettinger and Muller in 1955, who found that lowest trainability occurred 
dunng the winter months and highest trainability took place in summer and autumn, with a sharp drop in 
trainability at the onset of winter (Hettinger, 1961). This work suggested that the changes seemed to coincide 
with changes in the levels of ultraviolet radiation, especially since exposure of athletes to artificial ultraviolet
6
313


######## PDF idx 325 (printed 314) ########
SUPERTRAINING
light during the winter eliminated the observed changcs in trainability. In fact, the book by Hettinger which 
quoted these studies (7he Physiology o f Strength), like some of the early work by DeLorme, still remains one of 
the best pioneering texts on popularised scientific strength training, with the team of Hettinger and Muller 
undertaking many studies which were often well ahead of their time.
Another useful contribution was made by Letunov, who wrote an article ’Reflections on the Systematk 
Formulation of Training’ (Sovietsky Sport, 1950: 125) which strongly criticised the formulation of training 
regimes on the basis of the competition calendar alone. He felt that the stages of training were a consequence of 
biological processes, although he failed to appreciate that these processes, in turn, were modified by the training 
loads.
In England, Dyson was one of the first Westerners to popularise periodisation by using his knowledge of 
Eastern and Western training methods to write a textbook A New System o f Training (1946), which delineated a 
five-phase system of pcriodisation for athletics:
1. Non-competitive preparation period (5 months) with activities like gym training and cross-country running
2. Pre-competitive period, the beginning of specific preparation (1 month).
3. Initial competitive period (6 weeks).
4. Main competitive period (6 weeks).
5. Post-competitive period (6 weeks).
Ways of Organising Training
The above summary of the emergence of periodisation as a means of organising training may create the 
impression that periodisation is the only type of organisation or that it is synonymous with the organisation or 
scheduling of training. This is far from the truth, since there are numerous ways of preparing an athlete for 
competition and classical methods of periodisation may not necessarily offer the best approach to training 
organisation. Training for all sport may be carried out in terms of two broad general categories:
• Use of the sport alone to develop fitness for the given sport
• Use of the sport and supplementary activities to develop fitness for the given sport.
In the first case, training uses both the sport as a entire entity and the various aspects of the sport to enhance 
fitness, such as selected movements and portions of the play. In the latter case, supplementary activities such as 
resistance training, running and jumping may be used to develop the most important fitness qualities (e.g. speed, 
speed-strength or muscular endurance) demanded by the sport. Today, the idea of 'cross training' with other 
sports is also popular for achieving this aim. Most of the supplementary training is usually carried out before the 
competitive season begins, with intermittent use of such training in small doses to maintain the specific fitness 
qualities. Both of these categories of training require some or other form of organisation, one of the approaches 
being to rely strictly on periodisation.
Whichever system of organisation is chosen, the underlying principle to be applied is that o f optimal stress 
and restoration (see 1.16). This entails designing a physical training programme which stresses the body in such 
a way as to cause the appropriate form of supercompensatory adaptation, facilitated by regular use of restorative 
means to optimise the process and by regular enhancement of motor skills through nervous stimulation. To 
summarise what was covered in detail in 1.16, each training stimulus acts as a stressor which causes an acute 
(short-term) and a delayed response. If the stressor is of suitable intensity and duration, the restorative measures 
are adequate and subsequent stimuli (in the workout, microcycle or mesocycle) are applied at the most 
advantageous time of the stress recovery curve, then supercompensation and adaptation at a higher level of 
performance will follow. With special regard to strength training, Hettinger (1961) pointed out the following 
features of training which stimulate supcrcompcnsation. It is interesting to note that, although these points have 
been modified and extended by more recent research, they still offer useful information for the general strength 
training world today:
1. Production of adequate muscle tension is central to all muscic training
2. The maximum training benefits are derived by using muscle tension of no less than 40-50% of one’s 1RM
3. Maximum training effect does not require prolonging muscle tension to the point of fatigue
4. One single maximal strength effort per day is sufficient to maintain progress
Division of the sporting year into preparatory and competitive phases emerged logically from the experience of 
coaches and athletes, a distinction which creates the false impression that no preparation occurs during the
314


######## PDF idx 326 (printed 315) ########
SUPERTRAINING
competitive phase and no competition occurs during the preparatory phase. In team sports or track-and-field, the 
season is often so prolonged that this distinction cannot always be applied with such purity. Competitions may 
serve as a form of testing, controlled training or specific preparation; moreover, there are regular transition phases 
between preparatory stages and competitions over a prolonged season.
It can also be misleading to state categorically that there is a generalised training model for each sport. As 
in all scientific disciplines, several models may be possible, depending on many factors, including the situation, 
the individual, the variables and the period. Effective modem programming is a science and art which involves 
creativity, flexibility, individuality and understanding. Contingency plans should also be available to cope with 
unexpected or unplanned situations such as injury, loss of motivation, premature stagnation, changes in the rules, 
changes in the competitive roster, and personal trauma.
Implementation of the principle of specificity (see 1.3) is vital to the success of training, with high intensity 
sport-specific training under competitive circumstances (known as event-specific training) during both the 
preparatory and competition phases being an integral part of the programme. 
It is inadequate to train 
conservatively throughout the preparatory stage and the early competitive phase, deliberately avoiding stressful 
competitive situations in an attempt to produce maximal supercompensation with minimum injury by a specific 
date. Part of sport specific preparation is training under conditions which simulate those of the actual event so 
that one can cope efficiently with the demands of competition.
The precise balance between event-specific, sport-specific and general training is determined by the type of 
sport and the individual. For example, supplementary training (sport-specific and general training) for speed- 
strength and strength sports should constitute about 50-60% of the total work, whereas in distance endurance 
events, this type of training should constitute no more than about 20-30% of the work load.
Considerable research and experience has shown that the system of using the sport alone to develop 
proficiency generally is less effective than the integrated system of sport and supplementary training, although 
there seem to be notable exceptions in certain sports such as gymnastics. However, this is not necessarily an 
indictment of the use of strength training in some situations; more often than not it reflects a lack of adequate 
information and experience in this regard. The main ways in which an adjunct strength training system may be 
applied are as follows:
• Non-quantitative supplementary training consisting of general preparatory exercises precedes the competitive 
period, during which predominantly event-specific training is done. No calculations of training intensity or 
volume are made for prescribing the stages of training, although sports results or IRMs may be used to 
modify the programme.
• Non-quantitativc supplementary training comprising a general preparatory phase and a special preparatory 
phase precedes the competitive phase, during which predominantly event-specific training is done. No 
calculations of training intensity or volume are made for prescribing and monitoring the various stages of 
training, although sports results or IRMs may be used to modify the programme.
• Some form of long-term pcriodisation is applied. Calculations of training intensity and volume arc made to 
ensure that certain performance goals are attained at given stages of the long-term programme.
Before any serious discussion on periodisation begins, it is relevant to deal with the contention by 
some 
authorities that this cycled method of training organisation is unnecessary. It is quite true that many athletes have 
excelled with other methods, but this is not to say that all variants of periodisation need to be dismissed out of 
hand. On the contrary, some Western research which regards periodisation as a special version of the progressive 
overload principle is now beginning to corroborate the findings of Russian workers. The alternation o f heavy, 
medium and light days and phases alone would appear to facilitate recovery and adaptation to heavy loading 
more effectively than the use of monotonic increasing loading from phase to phase. Here, the heavy training days 
would strongly activate the relevant muscles, while the alternate lower intensity days would minimise the chance 
of overtraining or impaired restoration (Fry et al, 1994a; Fry et al, 1994b). Other research has shown the 
importance of periodising variations in training, especially as the latter becomes more demanding (Kraemer & 
Koziris 1992, Kraemer & Koziris 1994, Hakinnen 1989, Hakinnen & Komi 1986, Hakinnen & Pakarincn 1993a, 
Hakinnen & Pakarinen 1993b).

6.2 Periodisation as a Form of Organisation
As defined briefly in earlier chapters, the overall long-term cyclic structuring of training and practice to maximise 
performance to coincide with important competitions is known as periodisation (sec 1.14, 5.3 and 5.4).
Definitions and Fundamental Concepts
It is interesting to note that at least one Biblical quotation contains in colloquial terms some of the mos 
fundamental concepts of periodisation or cycled training, namely Ecclesiastes 3:
"There is a time for everything and a season fo r every activity under heaven . . .
A time to tear down and a time to build. . .
A time to search atui a time to give up . . .
A time to keep and a time to throw away.
A time to tear and a time to mend . .. "
The periodisation approach organises all training in terms of several basic structural units, namely the training 
session (the fundamental unit), the training day, the microcycle, the mesocycle, the macrocycle, the Olympic (or 
quadrennial) cycle and the multi-year cycle.
The microcycle refers to a number of training sessions which form a recurrent unit with a period of several 
days. 
Its minimum content is two different types of workout. 
The training day comprises one or more 
interrelated training sessions, with Bulgarian weightliftcrs commonly using in excess of 5 sessions per day, six 
days a week, each session comprising a few key exercises. The ntesocycle refers to a number of microcycles 
which serve as a recurring unit over a period of several weeks or months, while a macrocycle (which refers to a 
single competitive season) comprises a number of mcsocycles occupying a period of many months. It should be 
noted that earlier Russian literature, in contravention of the meaning of the prefixes meso- (middle) and macro- 
(large), used the term macrocycle to refer to what is now known as a mesocycle and vice versa. Any reader who 
may concurrently be referring to older Russian material should bear in mind that the above linguistically 
corrected meanings for the various training cycles are used in this text. The multi-year plan usually refers to a 
period exceeding that of the Olympic cycle.
More quantitatively, the microcycle typically has a duration of about 5-10 days; the mesocycle, a duration of 
1-4 months; and the macrocycle, 10-12 months. The term 'large macrocycle' sometimes is also used and may 
refer, for instance, to the training period of four years between successive Olympic Games or the several years 
taken to raise the level of qualification of an athlete from one Class to the next highest. Multi-year planning can 
include the latter type of macrocycle, but more characteristically, this term refers to the long-term organisation of 
an athlete's career as a junior or senior competitor or of the athlete's entire competitive lifespan. Three major 
phases of all training are recognised conventionally: preparation, competition and post-competition.
The contents and characteristics of each cycle are determined by the specific goals or results desired at the 
end of the cycle concerned. One has to be extremely carefully not to devise training units or programmes which 
try to develop any motor abilities or types of fitness which interfere with one another, as has been discussed 
earlier. Sometimes the coach may also attempt to develop too many or all types of fitness required by a given 
sport, thereby contravening the heterochronicity principle of development of the different motor abilities (see 
2.2.3 and later 6.10).
Various transition phases are often recognised between each of the major phases, with the post-competition 
phase often being regarded as the main transition phase, being used mainly for restoration. Some authorities 
consider that one of the transition phases should be recognised as a conversion phase during which specialised 
training converts maximum strength either into speed-strcngth or strength-cndurance. Although this terminology 
superficially seems attractive and descriptive, it is scientifically inaccurate, since one type of strength or motor 
ability cannot change into another, as has been shown by considerable research into the specificity of adaptation. 
It is more accurate to state that a prior stage of maximal strength training may serve as the foundation upon which 
later training for speed-strength or endurance is based, a sequence which is fundamental to some systems of 
training, e.g. the conjugate sequence system (see 5.3).
Similarly, different types of microcyclc are sometimes identified, such as ordinary (the usual scheme of 
uniformly increasing loading), introductory (bringing the athlete up to the competition stage), restorative (after 
heavy loading), competitive (immediately before and including the competition), and shock or stress (stimulating 
the athlete out of a state of stagnation) microcycles (Matveyev, 1981). Shock microcycles typically arc used if
316


######## PDF idx 328 (printed 317) ########
SUPERTRAININC
the current programme is not eliciting adequate strength gains. Generally, the microcycle following a shock 
microcycle is of low intensity, although, some elite athletes may employ two sequential shock microcycles (a 
double shock microcycle). It is inadvisable to use more than 3-4 shock microcycles a year or more than one 
double shock microcycle a year because of the serious risk of overtraining or injury. It must be stressed that, if 
iny shock cycles are used, the application of formal restoration becomes even more important (Ch 8.6). Using 
these concepts, typical mesocycles may be constructed logically from these microcycles, as follows:
• ordinary > ordinary > shock > restorative
• ordinary > introductory > competitive > restorative
• shock > ordinary > shock > restorative
• restorative > ordinary > ordinary > restorative.
Mesocycles may also be defined similarly, including introductory (beginning the preparatory period), base (the 
main types for increasing specific functional abilities), control-preparatory (transitional between base and 
competitive types), pre-competitive (immediate preparation for competition), competitive, and intermediate 
(restorative) mesocyclcs (Matveyev, 1981). The intermediate mesocycles, sometimes further broken down into 
restorative-preparatory and restorative-maintenance mesocycles, usually offer systematic active rest to help the 
athlete recover after heavy loading. Sometimes, the restorative-maintenance mesocyclc is simply referred to as a 
maintenance phase used to stabilise the high level of preparedness achieved during preceding phases. Several 
experts recognise large mesocycles, which comprise a closely integrated system of smaller mesocycles each of 
which has specific training goals. Later in this text, the concept of concentrated loading mesocycles is covered in 
detail because of its special training potential for advanced athletes.
Each phase of periodisation may be described in terms of sequences of these mesocycles. For example, a 
preparatory phase for long-duration endurance sports may use the following scheme:
• Introductory > base (general preparatory, developing) > base (stabilising) > base (special preparatory, 
developing) > control-preparatory > base > pre-competitive.
Speed-strength sports may have a preparatory phase structured in various other ways, for example:
• Introductory > base (developing > control-preparatory) > base (with pre-competitive elements).
• Introductory > base (general preparatory) > base (special preparatory) > pre-competitive.
Preparatory Phases of Training
As implied by the above discussion on mesocycles, the preparatory phase may be broken down further into GPP 
(General Physical Preparation) and SPP (Specialised Physical Preparation). 
However, it should always be 
remembered that the GPP and SPP always form an interconnected unit. In some cases, the GPP and SPP may 
even be concurrent or the GPP may be largely indistinguishable from the SPP (Bondarchuk, 1979).
The GPP is intended to provide balanced physical conditioning in endurance, strength, speed, flexibility and 
other basic factors of fitness, whereas the SPP concentrates on exercises which are more specific to the particular 
sport. 
Characteristically, the GPP may include participation in a variety of different physical activities which 
provide low intensity, all-round conditioning, with little emphasis on specific sporting skills. Participation in 
activities such as jogging, swimming, cycling, tennis or volleyball may be appropriate in this phase for some 
sports. If the player needs to gain muscle or lose excess fat, this is regarded as the appropriate period to do so. 
Sometimes an hypertrophy phase may be included in the GPP if there is a need for gaining functional muscle 
bulk. The decision to utilise this type of phase should be based on an assessment of the strength deficit discussed 
previously (Ch 1 and Fig 1.1).
Sometimes it is important to include very specific SPP-type exercises during the GPP either to rehabilitate 
any existing injuries or to eliminate any structural or functional deficiencies or imbalances in physique, posture 
and ncuromuscular skill. It may also be relevant to curtail or eliminate standard types of GPP from the training 
programme of anyone who is an advanced athlete or has trained regularly for a prolonged period at increasing 
levels of proficiency. Similarly, the use of GPP-type exercises may be appropriate for brief periods during the 
SPF to facilitate recovery or prevent stagnation. Moreover, the methods of GPP training are unsuitable for 
adequately or timeously stimulating improvements in performance among advanced athletes, whose trainability 
has already waned considerably over years of competition and whose continued growth depends on more specific 
or demanding methods.
