# Chernyak's Weekly Volume-Intensity Combinations for Strength-Speed Sports (Contested Inside the Book)

**What it is** — "Studies have shown that, in the annual macrocycle, the weekly levels of volume and intensity coincide fairly closely in sports requiring strength (Chernyak et al, 1979). Generally, the largest number of weeks involve medium volume and medium intensity, as well as weeks with high volume and high intensity." Chernyak's recommendations for strength-speed sports (PDF p. 343 / printed p. 332, verified against the page image):
1. "It is inadvisable always to combine low volume with low intensity, medium volume with medium intensity and large volume with high intensity."
2. "Training is most effective and least injurious if": medium volume, medium intensity "used most frequently (about 12-15 weeks per year)"; medium or high volume, low intensity next (9-10 weeks); low volume, medium intensity next (6-7 weeks).
3. Less often still: large volume, medium intensity (3-4 weeks); large volume, high intensity (2-3 weeks); low volume, high intensity (3-4 weeks); low volume, low intensity (1-2 weeks).

The authors add that overall volume and intensity "tell us little about the loading imposed in different intensity zones or at the level of individual muscle groups," nor about "the individual's perceived response," so attention must go to these and to "the level of mastery of the athlete" (PDF p. 343-344 / printed p. 332-333).

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given; the basis is Chernyak's research, summarised without data. Inference: rule 1's word "always" may mean "do not tie volume to intensity in lockstep," which would make it a rule against rigid coupling rather than against medium/medium weeks.

**When to apply** — As a rough annual budget of week types for strength-speed athletes: mostly medium/medium, then higher-volume low-intensity, then low-volume medium-intensity, with high-intensity weeks rare. Eric's baseline: "In-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 181, Inferred (transcript)), and "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... waving volume week to week" (line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: Chernyak's table gives a yearly frequency check on such waves.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book, same page, same question.** (a) The opening says the most frequent weeks are medium/medium "as well as weeks with high volume and high intensity," but recommendation 3 puts large volume with high intensity at only 2-3 weeks a year. (b) Recommendation 1 calls it inadvisable to "always" combine medium volume with medium intensity, while recommendation 2 makes medium/medium the most frequent week (12-15 weeks). One reading of (a) is that the opening describes observed practice and the recommendations prescribe change, but the text does not say so (Inference). Inference: the week ranges sum to about 36-45 weeks, not 52, so the remaining weeks are unaccounted for. No definitions of "low," "medium," "high" or "large" are given.

**Example** — The authors' own figures: about 12-15 medium/medium weeks, 9-10 medium-or-high volume with low intensity, 6-7 low volume with medium intensity, and only 2-3 large volume with high intensity in a strength-speed athlete's year (PDF p. 343 / printed p. 332).

# The Periodisation Controversy: Verkhoshansky's Critique of Classical Periodisation and Zheljazkov's Reply

**What it is** — Section 6.3 (PDF p. 344-346 / printed p. 333-335; verified against the page images) is Siff's voice by the book's own signals: it names Verkhoshansky in the third person throughout and refers to what "this textbook introduced." It has three voices.

**Siff's framing.** Classical Matveyev periodisation is widely used in the West, yet "even among Russian researchers and scientists, this approach to training has attracted some fierce criticism." Siff accepts part of it: the belief that periodisation is "an exact science" with computerised prescriptions is wrong, because "The body is not an exactly controlled, deterministic system"; training is "as much a matter of art, trial-and-error, and intuition, as it is of science," so schemes "should serve as approximate guidelines" modified by physiological and psychological markers (PDF p. 344 / printed p. 333). He concludes "organising training according to the classical model of Matveyev can be used only by athletes of low qualification for certain phases of the programme," the reason the book introduced ongoing subjective and objective assessment (PDF p. 345 / printed p. 334). He also objects that classical computation "utilises only two factors," volume and intensity.

**Verkhoshansky (1997), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "is not a suitable model for training for elite sportsmen" and should be "rejected or modified" for modern crowded calendars; "at best, separate forms of periodisation should be used by novice and young athletes." The mechanical division into periods and mesocycles rests on 1950s Soviet experience "mainly on the example of three sports, namely swimming, weightlifting, track and field athletics." Training should rest "much more on physiology." Plans should meet demands "distributed throughout a competitive season" rather than "notorious peaks of sports form." Kenyan runners "have never implemented periodisation"; British runners declined after adopting "Matveyev's block scheme" widely after 1980 (citing Horwill 1992, 1995; Tschiene 1991, 1992). He rejects "laws" of training and dismisses "'undulating models and 'wave models'" as "word play" (PDF p. 344-345 / printed p. 333-334).

**Zheljazkov (1998), as reported by Siff.** Periodisation "still managed to be utilised very effectively for many years in training numerous elite soviet and Eastern European athletes"; it is "erroneous" to treat Matveyev's concept as "the complete theory of sports training"; Verkhoshansky's charges of "primitive methodology" and "scholastic demagogy" are "a unprofessional personal attack"; national rises and falls in running are natural, not caused by periodisation. Classical periodisation "has not lost its fundamental importance" but has "serious qualitative limitations" to be modified by research on "exhaustion, adaptation and restoration," since regeneration is "nonlinear and heterochronical"; applied sport science "does not at all replace the entire concept of periodisation, but enriches it" (PDF p. 345-346 / printed p. 334-335).

**Why it works** — Each side argues from different evidence: Verkhoshansky from the 1950s origins of the model, its three-sport base and national running records; Zheljazkov from decades of Soviet and Eastern European elite success. Neither gives controlled data on these pages, and both national-results arguments are correlational (Inference).

**When to apply** — When a plan treats the annual chart as fixed. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)), and "in football you want to peak every Saturday" (line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: both sides would accept the roadmap framing, and Verkhoshansky's season-long demands point fits weekly football games better than a single peak.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Same question (is classical periodisation suitable for elite athletes), two named authorities, opposite answers, on PDF p. 344 versus p. 345. Note the internal tension with the book's own method: Verkhoshansky dismisses "undulating models" as word play (PDF p. 345), while the authors endorse heavy, medium and light alternation (PDF p. 326, 329); Inference: his complaint is about relabelling, not about load variation working, so it is a tension in emphasis, not a contradiction. This also touches Eric's baseline directly: "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Library sources: Issurin 2016 judged evidence for Verkhoshansky's own concentrated-unidirectional alternative insufficient for team sports ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]); Harries et al. 2015 found linear and undulating programmes give similar strength gains, and Afonso et al. 2019 argue that periodised-versus-non-periodised meta-analyses did not isolate periodisation's effect (vault research-papers entries). Inference: the modern papers support neither side's strong claim. Evans frames the same split as "classic" versus "non-classic" literature ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: Verkhoshansky's claim that British middle-distance runners won Olympic gold before, not after, adopting Matveyev's scheme widely after 1980, against Zheljazkov's reply that "all sports in all nations naturally undergo periods of ascendancy and decline" (PDF p. 344-345 / printed p. 333-334).

**Related** — [[framework--eight-weaknesses-of-the-matveyev-model]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[framework--six-broad-periodisation-schemes]], [[claim--heavy-medium-light-alternation-beats-monotonic-increasing-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], [[research-papers/harries-2015-systematic-review-and-meta-analysis-of-linear-and-undulating-periodized-resistance-trainin]], [[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]], [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]]

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

=== principle--programming-is-an-art-on-principles-not-an-algorithm
chapter: "6.17"
**What it is** — The chapter's closing section (PDF p. 403 / printed p. 392, checked against the page image): "it is unacceptable to understand programming as the following of some instructions which prescribe a rigid order in the organisation of training. Furthermore, it is also senseless to view it as the creation of a precise algorithm, as is done in chess. Programming in sport is an art based on specific principles, which allows the coach creative initiative in making the final decisions." The authors call the chapter "only the first steps," and leave to the coach "the sequence of loading in the mesocycles and their composition in the microcycles, as well as rational ways of combining the contents of these microcycles into a system... It is the role of the coach to solve such problems."

=== principle--technical-mastery-needs-competition-intensity-practice
chapter: "6.14.4"
**What it is** — The authors (PDF p. 399 / printed p. 388, checked against the page image): "technical mastery can be acquired only through practice with high intensity loading which simulates competition conditions. Proficiency gained under conditions of low stimulation and intensity do not usually transfer successfully to the maximal effort situations of top-level competition. This is relevant to the use of visualisation to perfect sporting movements; this technique is not very successful if it does not offer mental simulation of the movements, the feelings and the competitive circumstances under which the movements have to be displayed. Practice only makes perfect if one practises all components of the performance process under the conditions which mimic those of the sporting event as closely as possible." The same idea appears as the seventh primary aim, "Modelling competition activi

=== framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training
chapter: "6.15"
**What it is** — The authors recommend "the following sequence of logical operations, where each calculation is made by taking into account the calculation made in the preceding operation (Verkhoshansky, 1985)" (PDF p. 401 / printed p. 390, checked against the page image). The eight steps, with their key wording:
1. **Determine the progress in results and the dates.** "The calculations rely on a predictive model of the dynamics of the sport results relative to the competition calendar," based on "a multi-faceted objective assessment of the athlete's potential" and what is "realistically feasible in the current year at his level of mastery."
=== heuristic--set-mesocycle-boundaries-by-main-competition-dates
chapter: "6.14.5"
**What it is** — The authors' four practical principles for when the calendar and adaptation pull against each other (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389, checked against the page image). The conflict: "the dates of the main competitions may change radically, while the dates of traditional competitions remain the same. A worse situation arises if the competition season is extended and the length of the preparatory stages is shortened."
1. "Organisation of training should provide favourable conditions for promoting functional adaptation of the body within the constraints of the competition calendar. The calendar should be co-ordinated with the periods and duration of the mesocycles."
=== heuristic--choose-cross-training-by-fitness-qualities-and-phase-not-sport-label
chapter: "5.5"
**What it is** — The authors define Western "cross training" as "using relevant secondary sports to augment the training effect produced in an athlete's primary sport," and tie it to the two ways of combining training from 5.3: supplementary activities can be prescribed "concurrently with the athlete's main sport on the same day or during the same training phase or in a definite sequence where one supplementary activity gives way to another and finally to the main sport over a given period" (PDF p. 309 / printed p. 298). In Russia and Eastern Europe, they write, the choice "does not simply focus primarily on the type of sport used, but rather on the relationship between the motor and fitness qualities in the supplementary activities and the primary sport," with "qualitative and quantitative modelling of each sport involved so as to ensure that the supplementary sports do not impair perfo

**What it is** — Evans's slides (U3 L4 p.13-14), titled "Literature Issue," present two
opposing characterizations of the periodization research base, which the slides state (no
attribution shown). Non-classic literature (the slides' term for research not from Eastern Europe or the Soviet Union) is
described as: "Suggestive there is little research to support Periodization. Very few elite
athletes are used in the research. Short term studies. One dimensional. Non-classic believes
(most of the time) the CLASSIC literature is promoting linear periodization." Classic
literature is described as: "Large amount of insight to support the usage of a
multidimensional, planned approach. A lot of studies utilizing elite athletes. Long term
studies available." He then quotes L.P. Matveyev directly, dated 1977: "Wave oscillations
characterize load dynamics in both relatively small and more prolonged phases (stages,
periods) or the training process," offered as an example of what the classic literature
argues (a non-linear, "wave" model), in apparent contrast to the non-classic camp's alleged
belief that classic literature promotes strictly linear periodization. The following slide
(p.15) shows "Figure 7: Matveyev's Classic Model of an Annual Training Plan," with red arrows
highlighting the "daily, microcycle, and mesocycle fluctuations" in volume, intensity and
technical training; p.16 then states directly, "Non-linear in CLASSIC literature."

**Why it works** — Evans does not name specific non-classic authors, studies, or a specific
review supporting either characterization; this is his own summary framing of a two-sided
debate, not a mechanism claim. Evans's own position is explicit: classic periodization is
non-linear (p.16), illustrated by Matveyev's model with fluctuations highlighted (p.15).
